On examination, her mental status and cranial nerves were normal. She had normal muscle strength in all groups but there was axial and proximal stiffness in lower limbs, with spasms and delayed muscle relaxation after voluntary activation; the right leg was more affected than the left.
Over the previous year, she had been assessed for fatigue, dyspareunia, anxiety and insomnia.
Her gait was unstable with slow steps, extended legs, broad base, lumbar hyperlordosis and poor girdle swing.
Extrapyramidal and cerebellar tests were normal.
She reported mild allodynia wherever her body was rubbed, but there was no objective deficit or any sensory modality.

extractions.quote: The diagnosis of stiff-person syndrome is clinical (stiffness and painful muscle spasms) supported by electrophysiology studies (continuous motor unit activity in agonist and antagonist muscles) and exclusion of other feasible causes. Additional minor criteria are the specific autoantibodies and the response to benzodiazepines.

Given the positive anti-amphiphysin antibodies, we requested mammography, which showed a suspicious lesion in the upper outer quadrant of the right breast (figure 2). Ultrasound scan of breast confirmed three nodular lesions of approximately 1 cm3 and several axillary lymph nodes.

A thick needle biopsy of the main lesion and fine-needle aspiration of an adenopathy provided histopathology, which showed an infiltrating ductal carcinoma of intermediate cytological grade, with positive immunostaining for hormonal and HER2 receptors and lymph node involvement.
